doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Slow trio work, word of mouth and Max Gordon
summary: Other musicians and club owners got him work; Harry Colomby put him into the Vanguard.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So in 1958 you have this first leader gig, and then I’d imagine that you started working more and more as a leader.
It was slow at first. The trio album...the trio work was slow at first. It later became more popular.

I think what you always said, it was other musicians who got you work all the time. Musicians whom he played with... I mean, he was always getting calls from other musicians who had a club where they wanted to book him. I know that he always said that that’s how he got known, was through word-of-mouth from other musicians.
So they recognized your voice, your artistic voice before the general public did, in a certain way.
Well, the piano playing was part of it. That was always part of it.
Well, and club owners liked you, too. Club owners always liked you because you were so dependable and so nice.
Max Gordon I used to work for every so often, and he put me in there... Colomby got me in there.
Although that happened a little later, if we’re going to position this chronologically.
Reading Monk’s biography, I think he got involved with Monk in the early ‘60s...
